document_check.note: Document is Kim SK, Kim H, Kim SH, Kim JB, Kim L, 'Electroencephalography-based classification of Alzheimer's disease spectrum during computer-based cognitive testing', Scientific Reports 2024;14:5252, doi:10.1038/s41598-024-55656-8. It reports 58 patients (20 SCD, 10 naMCI, 18 aMCI, 10 AD) classified from resting-state and memory-encoding EEG. This matches the cited Kim et al. 2024 comparison of acquisition states.

cited_result: Four-class (SCD, naMCI, aMCI, AD) EEG classification performance compared by acquisition state within one sample of 58 patients. Memory-encoding EEG outperformed resting-state EEG in all models; the best model (cKNN) reached 93.10% accuracy on encoding data versus 67.24% on resting data, evaluated with leave-one-subject-out.
tool_reason: The cited result is the discrimination of machine-learning classifiers and the ranking of feature sets or acquisition states, so PROBAST applies, with the PROBAST+AI considerations.

domains.rationale: The paper does not say how participants were sampled (consecutive, random or by diagnostic group) and reports no eligibility criteria. It gives only the recruitment total, two exclusions, and that participants were patients at one hospital. The group sizes (20/10/18/10) and the absence of a consecutive-series description leave open a group-based (case-control type) selection.

domains.rationale: All participants had EEG recorded on the same 64-channel system under the same protocol, and preprocessing (including ICA artefact correction) was automated. EEG is available when the model would be used.

domains.rationale: The four labels were assigned by clinical staging (CDR and SNSB-II memory z-score), with no biomarker confirmation of AD pathology, although the paper calls ATN the gold standard. The stated rule (CDR 0 = SCD, 0.5 = MCI, 1 = AD) conflicts with the group CDR values in Table 2. SCD has a mean CDR of 0.21 and AD a mean of 0.67, so the labels were not assigned consistently by the stated definition. The paper does not report the interval between clinical labelling and EEG recording, or whether labelling was blind to EEG.

domains.rationale: There are 58 participants (10 in each of the two smallest classes) and 2268 to 2772 candidate features per state. Features were selected by univariable ANOVA across the four groups, and a single fixed feature set is reported (56 resting, 258 encoding), meaning selection was done on the full data set outside the LOSO folds. That is leakage. It may also favour the encoding condition, which contributed more candidate features and more selected features from the same 58 people. The best of 12 models was then picked on its test-set F1, with no separate held-out set; the paper does not explain what the 'validation' results are under LOSO. No calibration, no handling of class imbalance, no hyperparameter reporting and no external validation. The only mitigations are the participant-level split (LOSO) and ridge weighting.

overall: High risk of bias (PROBAST: analysis high, outcome high, participants unclear, predictors low)
overall_rationale: A high rating in any domain makes the overall rating high. The analysis domain is high because of univariable feature selection on the full data set before leave-one-subject-out evaluation, 58 participants for thousands of candidate features, best-model selection on test results, no calibration and no external validation. This leakage bears directly on the cited encoding-versus-resting comparison, because the encoding condition had more candidate and selected features. The outcome labels are also inconsistent with the stated CDR rule.

applicability.rationale: Patients at a single Korean hospital spanning SCD to AD, with no cognitively normal controls. The sample is small, and the groups differ in age and education.
The four classes are clinical stages (CDR and SNSB-II) without amyloid or tau confirmation, whereas the paper frames the aim as classifying AD pathology.
